item.title: A Control Barrier Function-Constrained Model Predictive Control Framework for Safe Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2604.06463v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensuring safety under unknown and stochastic dynamics remains a significant challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). In this paper, we propose a model predictive control (MPC)-based safe RL framework, called Probabilistic Ensembles with CBF-constrained Trajectory Sampling (PECTS), to address this challenge. PECTS jointly learns stochastic system dynamics with probabilistic neural networks (PNNs) and control barrier functions (CBFs) with Lipschitz-bounded neural networks. Safety is enforced by incorporating learned CBF constraints into the MPC formulation while accounting for the model stochasticity. This enables probabilistic safety under model uncertainty. To solve the resulting MPC problem, we utilize a sampling-based optimizer together with a safe trajectory sampling method that discards unsafe trajectories based on the learned system model and CBF. We also derive a finite-horizon exit-probability bound using tail information for centered barrier increments. We validate PECTS in various simulation studies, where it outperforms baseline methods.
item.dc:creator: Ali Umut Kaypak, Prashanth Krishnamurthy, Farshad Khorrami

item.title: RCOA Extension and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2607.02797v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Relaxed Convex Obstacle Avoidance (RCOA) formulation is the first approach to enable a fully convex optimal control problem (OCP) for obstacle avoidance. Convergence analysis of RCOA yields an analytical framework that defines a unique characteristic: the ability to maintain obstacle avoidance (OA) efficacy even when obstacles reside beyond the controller's prediction horizon. In this paper, RCOA is extended to three-dimensional environments and apply it to Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) navigation. Furthermore, the formulation is enhanced to incorporate vehicle geometries, moving beyond point-mass representations to enable collision avoidance between 3D objects. Numerical simulations demonstrate that RCOA provides computational performance on par or exceeding state-of-the-art methods. Notably, RCOA is demonstrated to enable a Nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) to execute aggressive maneuvers through narrow passages with reduced prediction horizons, ensuring real-time feasibility at frequencies exceeding 30~Hz.

item.title: A Theory of Information Architecture for Networked Decisions: Freshness, Locality, and Coordination
item.description: arXiv:2609.06351v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A broader view of a network can help agents coordinate, but collecting that view takes time. When is a fresh local observation more useful than an older view of the whole network, and when should an agent look only partway across it? We study agents that repeatedly minimize a shared quadratic cost in an environment that evolves independently of their actions. An information architecture specifies what each agent observes and how old those observations are. Each agent uses a synchronized neighborhood snapshot, so extending its scope also ages the nearby readings used in the decision. We assume that the optimal action with complete information is affine in the state, and that the conditional mean of the current state equals the old state scaled by a common exponential decay factor. Using the classical Marschak--Radner decomposition, we derive the delay threshold beyond which fresh local information outperforms a complete but older global view. This comparison allows non-Gaussian states and nonlinear decision rules. We then determine how far an agent should look by balancing the benefit of additional observations against their greater age. In a Gaussian spatial model on a line, we derive the optimal observation radius: looking beyond the local node pays only when information travels more than twice the spatial correlation length in one coherence time. The preferred information architecture also depends on the decision being made. On a fixed 64-node ring, increasing only the reach of the decision weights from 0.7 to 6 hops shifts the optimal observation radius from one to five hops.
item.dc:creator: Scott Moeller, Bhaskar Krishnamachari

item.title: Contract-Based Decomposition of Temporal Logic Specifications for Networked Systems under Arbitrary Partitions
item.description: arXiv:2609.23579v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Computational complexity is an inherent limitation of formal synthesis for networked systems, and decomposing the global specification into local ones relaxes this limitation at the cost of conservatism. Since the granularity of the partition governs this trade-off, it is reasonable to treat the partition as a design variable, which calls for local specifications that remain correct for every partition. To this end, this paper gives each agent a local specification, written as an assume-guarantee contract that the agent can establish from local information. We first derive a necessary and sufficient condition for these contracts to decompose the global specification under a given partition. Building on this, we then present a condition under which the decomposition is correct for every partition, so that the partition becomes a free design variable. For linear dynamics and signal temporal logic formulas with affine predicates, we further synthesize a controller for each coalition by a tube-based approach. Finally, simulations on a network of input-coupled tanks show how the choice of partition trades computational cost against conservatism.

item.title: Symbolic-Permutation-Based Direct Sparse Jacobian Assembly for Accelerated Power-Flow Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.12654v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The repeated assembly of the sparse Jacobian matrix constitutes a primary computational bottleneck in the Newton-Raphson power-flow analysis. Through an algebraic operator equivariance analysis of the Jacobian matrix, this paper formalizes the reduction process and proposes a direct sparse Jacobian assembly method based on symbolic permutation. By pre-applying the permutation to the admittance matrix during a fast one-time symbolic phase via its sparse prefix-sum property, the runtime bus-type projection overhead and indirect mapping caches are entirely eliminated. Consequently, complex Jacobian differentiation and global matrix assembly fuse into a single operation, yielding a single-pass, branchless algorithm that streams values directly into contiguous memory. The proposed algorithm is implemented in the open-source RustPower solver. Benchmarks on IEEE test systems and PEGASE 9241 demonstrate that the proposed assembly is 28.1-37.9 times faster than the MATPOWER-style baseline and 8.9-9.7 times faster than the in-house Sch\"afer-Braun-inspired assembly (V1); on PEGASE 9241, it outperforms optimized traditional C++ assembly routines by 3.72 times in cold construction and 2.59 times across iterations. End-to-end, the iteration-loop solve time with KLU is 1.16-1.97 times faster than the native C++ LightSim2Grid and up to 95.5 times faster than pandapower, while leaving numerical results and convergence behavior unchanged. The method extends directly to general problems where a sparse Jacobian inherits its structure from a static network operator, including transient stability analysis, EMT simulation, and OPF Hessian assembly.

item.title: A Variational Latent Equilibrium for Learning in Neuronal Circuits
item.description: arXiv:2603.09600v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Brains remain unrivaled in their ability to recognize and generate complex spatiotemporal patterns. While AI is able to reproduce some of these capabilities, deep learning algorithms remain largely at odds with our current understanding of brain circuitry and dynamics. This is prominently the case for backpropagation through time (BPTT), the go-to algorithm for learning complex temporal dependencies. In this work we propose a general formalism to approximate BPTT in a controlled, biologically plausible manner. Our approach builds on, unifies and extends several previous approaches to local, time-continuous, phase-free spatiotemporal credit assignment based on principles of energy conservation and extremal action. Our starting point is a prospective energy function of neuronal states, from which we calculate real-time error dynamics for time-continuous neuronal networks. With this, as a first contribution we provide a simple and straightforward derivation of the adjoint method dynamical equations, the time-continuous equivalent to BPTT. Importantly, additional approximations are necessary to avoid unphysical temporal non-localities. One such approximation was recently proposed in Generalized Latent Equilibrium (GLE), but enforcing temporal locality of the backpropagating dynamics induces an error in the gain that becomes problematic when processing complex signals. Thus, our second contribution is to design a learning rule for the backward weights to find a fully local (in space and time) set of equations for neuron and synapse dynamics that corrects for this gain difference. With this inclusion of backward weight learning, our theory provides a rigorous framework for spatiotemporal deep learning in the brain, while simultaneously advancing a blueprint for physical circuits capable of carrying out these computations.

item.title: Stealthy, High-Impact False Data Injection Attacks in Smart Grid Using Physics-Constrained GAN with Limited System Knowledge
item.description: arXiv:2611.15162v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: False data injection (FDI) attacks can distort power system state estimation while retaining plausible measurement patterns. Existing FDI methods trade stealth for impact or vice versa. They often assume access to internal grids, all-bus sensing, or defender models. In this paper, we propose a detector-agnostic physics-constrained generative adversarial network (PCGAN) that learns decoupled power-flow sensitivities from historical measurements of deployed sensors. The learned active-power-angle and reactive-power-voltage-magnitude relationships guide perturbations restricted to compromised channels, while adversarial training promotes realistic spatiotemporal patterns. We implement PCGAN and seven existing FDI attacks on the IEEE 300-bus system using one year of observed hourly demand from PJM Interconnection, a regional transmission organization in the United States, and synthetic bus-level load profiles. We compare their performance across 10%, 30%, 60%, and 100% compromised sensors. Attack stealth is assessed against ten machine-learning (ML) detectors and conventional bad-data detection (BDD) methods, while physical impact is quantified through nonlinear alternating-current weighted least-squares state estimation. PCGAN achieves 84.28% mean ML evasion and 22.31% mean spatial load misperception across the four scenarios. Its mean stealth-impact trade-off score reaches 18.69%, compared with 5.61% for the strongest competing attack. PCGAN also achieves 83.45% chi-square BDD evasion and 86.02% largest-normalized-residual BDD evasion. These results demonstrate a favorable stealth-impact balance under varying sensor-access levels and provide challenging attack cases for evaluating FDI detectors.
